analysis.one_liner: Bars federal agencies from requiring public access to research they fund.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Judiciary Committee when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have changed copyright law to stop federal agencies from attaching one specific condition to research grants: requiring that the results be made publicly available rather than kept behind a publisher's paywall. It applied to any work connected to a federal funding agreement that also got money or input from outside entities — which covers most published papers from federally funded science. In practice, it would have barred policies like the National Institutes of Health rule that requires grant-funded papers to be posted in a free public database within a year of publication.
analysis.who_benefits: Commercial and scientific-society journal publishers would gain the most: their subscription paywalls over government-funded research would be legally protected, since no agency could require public release of the papers. Publishers would keep selling access to research the public already paid for through taxes, and researchers would keep full copyright control over their articles.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Journal publishers and their subscribers' fees

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any federal agency from imposing, as a condition of a research grant or contract, any term requiring transfer or license of copyright rights in a related published work, including rights over the work's public availability [S2][S3].
Also bars agencies from requiring grantees to waive those protections or from asserting government rights that would limit a publisher's copyright in the work [S2][S3].
Applies to funding agreements entered into after enactment, and requires the Copyright Office to report in five years on how the restriction affected access to research [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers who funded the research would bear the cost: results from billions of dollars in federal science funding would sit behind subscription paywalls. Patients, physicians, small institutions, and independent researchers who cannot afford journal subscriptions would lose access to findings their taxes paid for, and other agencies would be blocked from adopting public-access policies like the NIH's.

drawbacks.text: Publishers argue that peer review, editing, and journal infrastructure cost real money, and that giving papers away free undercuts the subscriptions that fund those services [S3].

The bill does not distinguish between purely federally funded work and work with genuine non-federal input, so 'extrinsic work' would sweep in most published papers from federal grants, potentially eliminating public-access mandates across the government [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's main effect is a transfer of control over publicly funded research to private publishers, at the direct expense of the taxpayers who paid for that research. The publishers' cost argument — that journals need revenue to organize peer review — is genuine, but the bill would have settled it permanently in publishers' favor by outlawing the alternative rather than balancing access against publishing costs. It would have undone the one federal policy (NIH's) that already provided free public access to funded medical research.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or a vote, and expired when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers Jr. (D-MI) introduced the bill on September 9, 2008, joined by Reps. Darrell Issa (R-CA), Robert Wexler (D-FL), and Tom Feeney (R-FL) [S1][S3].
The same day, it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee — the only committee action it ever received [S5].

The bill would have barred federal agencies from conditioning research funding on making the resulting published works publicly available, and from requiring waiver of copyright rights in such works [S2][S3].
No hearing, markup, or vote ever followed; the record shows no further action after the sponsor's introductory remarks on September 10, 2008 [S5].
The bill died automatically when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers, patients, and the research community are better off: agencies can still require that government-funded research be made publicly available, and publishers did not get federal open-access mandates barred by law.

for.name: John Conyers Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar agencies from requiring public release of federally funded research works.

for.name: Darrell Issa, Robert Wexler, and Tom Feeney
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's three cosponsors (two Republicans, one Democrat).

for.name: Commercial and scientific-society journal publishers
for.role: Publishers of subscription journals (notably the American Chemical Society)
for.what_they_did: Publicly backed the bill and its successor versions as protection for their subscription revenue against open-access mandates.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; took no action
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; sponsorship was bipartisan, with two Republicans and one Democrat joining the Democratic sponsor.

industries.note: The bill would lock in the subscription paywall model as the permanent channel for federally funded research by making it unlawful for agencies to require public release. Publishers' revenue comes from selling access to work taxpayers already funded.

Grantees would keep full copyright control of their papers, but they would lose the leverage of agencies' public-access requirements — and researchers are also the main readers who benefit from free access to each other's work.
